These figures come from the Mem0 paper (*Mem0. Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory*, `llm/memory/agent/`). The Zep paper in the folder doesn't measure its memory size on LoCoMo, so Zep's numbers here are Mem0's measurements of Zep.

**Memory stored per LoCoMo conversation (average)**, from Section 4.5, p. 14:

| System | Tokens stored as memory |
|---|---|
| Mem0 (plain, natural-language memories) | about 7k |
| Mem0 with graph memory | about 14k, roughly double, because it adds nodes and their relationships |
| Zep | more than 600k |
| Raw conversation, no memory layer | about 26k |

- So Mem0 stores about a quarter of the raw conversation, and Mem0 with graph memory stores about half. Zep's graph is more than 20 times the size of the raw conversation (p. 14).
- The paper says Zep's graph is so large because it keeps a full summary at every node and also stores facts on the edges between nodes. This repeats the same information across the graph (p. 14).
- The 26k raw figure matches the dataset description: 10 conversations, each with about 600 dialogue turns and 26,000 tokens on average (p. 6).

**How soon Zep's new memories can be retrieved** (p. 14):
- When the authors searched right after adding memories to Zep, the searches often failed to answer the queries correctly.
- The same searches run again **several hours later** gave much better results.
- The authors put this delay down to Zep building its graph in the background with several asynchronous LLM calls. They conclude this makes Zep impractical for real-time use.
- By comparison, Mem0 finishes building its graph memory in **under a minute** even in the worst case, so new memories can be used right away.

This is Mem0's own report on a competing system. The Zep paper doesn't address the delay.
